transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

On your Bosch SMS25AW00G, E:09 typically indicates a flow-through heating element or circuit fault. Regarding cost, this is usually not an extremely expensive fix; it involves replacing either the heater assembly (often integrated with the circulation pump) or the temperature sensor, which are standard components. However, to be sure we aren't looking at a simple settings issue or a different problem, I need to confirm the nature of the fault. Please run an intensive or 65°C programme next time and let me know: are the dishes and wash water clearly cold, or just wet?
Both the hot programme and eco have come out cold. The water felt cold to touch mid-cycle too, not just the dishes.

Since the water was clearly cold mid-cycle and both programmes failed to heat, this suggests a genuine heating fault rather than just poor drying. The E:09 code on your Bosch SMS25AW00G specifically points to the flow-through heater assembly (which is integrated with the circulation pump in this model) or its associated temperature sensor. This is not an extremely expensive fix; it typically involves replacing that single heater/pump unit, which is a standard component. You should be able to get this replaced by an engineer for a reasonable call-out and parts charge, or if you are handy, the part itself is reasonably priced.
Ok, but the machine is 9 years old so I'm weighing up repair vs replace. Roughly what would the part cost? I do have a multimeter if there's a safe way to test the heater first.

To confirm whether it is most likely the heater assembly (and not just a sensor), we can test it safely with your multimeter. Please switch off and unplug the dishwasher first. You will need to remove the lower rack and filter cover to access the circulation pump/heater unit at the bottom of the tub. Disconnect the electrical connector from that unit, then use your multimeter on the resistance (Ohms) setting to measure across the two main terminals of the heater element itself. A healthy heater usually reads between 20–40 Ohms; if it shows 'OL' or infinity, the heating element is open-circuit and needs replacing.

Ok, I did the test with it unplugged and the panel off. The multimeter shows open circuit across the heater terminals on the pump. So what would the part cost roughly, and is it worth fixing on a 9 year old machine?

An open-circuit reading suggests the heating element inside that flow-through assembly has failed. On a 9-year-old machine, the decision is yours; if other components like the door seals and spray arms are in good condition, repairing just the heater is often more economical than replacing the whole appliance, provided you can get the part fitted.
Thanks, but you still haven't said roughly what the part would cost. Do you have a ballpark figure for the heater/pump unit, and what an engineer would charge to fit it?

[Heading: Likely cause: heater element]
